# How This Book Is Written {.unnumbered}

A book about AI-assisted engineering should be explicit about its authoring methodology. I am writing this synthesis during an academic sabbatical at Harvard University while spending dedicated time at ETH Zürich, with the goal of bringing a fully polished volume to completion by the end of 2027. Releasing early drafts in the open is uncomfortable, but it creates a powerful form of personal accountability. When colleagues, students, and critical readers can see a manuscript taking shape, it forces every section to stand on hard evidence. Working with generative systems every day quickly exposes both their practical utility and inherent failure modes.

The ideas behind this book grew out of our foundations paper on Architecture 2.0 [@ReddiYazdanbakhsh2025Architecture20]. That article set out the broad vision for using AI across system and chip design. Bringing computer architecture, machine learning, and electronic design automation together into a single engineering argument required years of incremental work. These three domains answer to different physical realities and evidence standards, and connecting them requires more than a clever prompt.

To write this book, I apply the exact pedagogical principles we teach inside it, a methodology refined through Harvard's Learning Incubator (LInc) program. Every chapter begins with backward design [@WigginsMcTighe2005BackwardDesign]: I start by defining the core questions, tradeoffs, and lasting principles, establish the evidence requirements, and write the explanatory prose last.

I treat generative models not as authors, but as an expansive information vault, reminiscent of the paradigm shift in web search two decades ago. These generative systems provide the breadth of an interactive encyclopedia, allowing me to probe creative alternatives, examine interdisciplinary literature, and surface historical connections that would otherwise require years of manual survey. Yet an information vault possesses no architectural taste, no physical intuition, and no engineering accountability. The purpose of a synthesis monograph is not the passive accumulation of information; it is defending a technical perspective that survives physical, tooling, and organizational constraints.

To turn exploration into a disciplined manuscript, I use an authoring flow built around specialized review roles. Simulated learner panels test pedagogical clarity and intuition. Senior architect panels push on technical rigor and physical constraints. Systems panels check tool interfaces and synthesis assumptions. Citation auditors trace claims, benchmark figures, and equations back to primary papers. Custom linters enforce house style rules, keeping the prose active, direct, and unpadded. As shown in @fig-author-ai-workflow, these review panels feed into an automated build harness that compiles the manuscript, checks references, and verifies formatting.

![**The AI-assisted authoring engine as a multi-agent design loop.** Backward design establishes intent first. The generation swarm communicates across a shared inter-agent bus to propose drafts, while simulated review panels supply critique. The human author in the central hub functions with in-order commit authority over what reaches the deterministic validation harness. System architects will recognize a structural parallelism to a modern out-of-order CPU datapath: Stage 1 acts as frontend fetch and decode, the agent swarms act as parallel execution units, and the central author hub acts as the reorder buffer and commit stage holding 100% retirement authority.](images/F0-author-ai-workflow.svg){#fig-author-ai-workflow width="100%" fig-alt="Architecture diagram showing Stage 1 Backward Design, Stage 2 Human-in-the-Loop Core and Simulated Agent Review Panels, Stage 3 Validation Harness."}

Operating an AI-assisted authoring pipeline rapidly reveals that generation speed does not equal synthesis quality. In an early chapter draft, an agent swarm generated thirty pages of fluent prose about hardware-software co-design in under two minutes. Yet upon close inspection, the text subtly erased the distinction between cycle-accurate simulator boundaries and physical signoff gates, floating smooth generalities where hard engineering trade-offs belonged. Overriding that draft required hours of manual pruning, rebuilding the evidence chain, and restoring strict technical definitions. As authors and architects, our primary contribution is not generating candidate text; it is maintaining the diagnostic taste and non-negotiable commit authority required to reject plausible slop.

Early drafts inevitably collect unrefined prose and speculative text. Catching ungrounded claims, accepting critique, and trimming the draft back to verifiable evidence is the core of the work. Generative systems produce options, but human judgment governs every decision. I decide which distinctions matter, what the evidence supports, where an analogy fails, and what must be cut. My role begins before anything is generated and ends only when I sign off on the final text.

Developing the manuscript alongside runnable reference code keeps the principles grounded in executable reality rather than abstract claims. While the manuscript and code are developed in the open, I keep the internal prompt orchestrations, subagent configurations, and rule files private. Just as a chip design team open-sources reference RTL while guarding internal PDK flows and physical design scripts, the engineering value lies in how the agentic machinery is governed to enforce rigor.

Writing is how I test whether I understand a subject well enough to teach it. When an explanation cannot survive a reader's questions, the synthesis is not finished. This remains a working manuscript, and I expect it to evolve as the evidence improves. If you spot a flaw, an imprecise claim, or a connection that needs a harder test, please reach out to me directly.

Vijay Janapa Reddi
*Harvard University / ETH Zürich*
